This work is not a technical paper, and I drafted it purely out of a genuine desire for a better conference experience. Even though I have tried my best to be the best reviewer possible — see selected examples in Appendix C, where I proactively engaged with other reviewers to converge on cleaner (and hopefully fairer) paper decisions — **I have never encountered another reviewer who initiates such discussions across the hundreds of papers I have reviewed.** This led me to believe that systematic incentives are required to encourage good reviewing practices, rather than merely writing well-intentioned words in reviewer guidance and hoping they will be followed.

While it is unfortunate that it was rejected, I consider this understandable as (1) its scores are not competitive; and (2) ICLR does not have a dedicated position track, so it is at least semi-fair to expect a higher standard.

---
## **However, I must respectfully note that the three remaining concerns highlighted in the metra-review are `materially inaccurate.`**

> `Area Chair vwKS`: “Reviewers raised the following criticisms: (1) ... Since the paper is not an experimental paper and lacks data, rebuttals were mostly a matter of opinion, with additional paper edits to address some issues. In general, **I do not think criticisms 2, 6, and 9 were addressed to a satisfactory extent.**”

Below is a walkthrough explaining why, for record-keeping purposes and future reference.

---

### ***(2) the paper doesn’t sufficiently address the possibility of AI helping solve these problems***

This concern is raised by Reviewer `uVmE`, but it is not about “AI helping solve these problems” (i.e., how to design a better conference review mechanism) as the AC claimed. Rather, it is about the reviewer wanting me to emphasize that AI assistant would contribute to an increased volume of research submissions, where this increase is one key root cause of why current review mechanisms often struggle.

> `uVme`: “…automated scientific discovery and AI's increasing role in performing research and writing papers. It focuses on the symptom, the increase in submissions, rather than addressing the cause, which includes AI and automated research and writing.”

**The meta-review interpreted this concern in a completely hallucinated fashion** (likely because I heavily discussed the unreliability of AI-powered review helpers elsewhere).

That said, it never hurts to have a more complete story. To this point — clearly attributing submission volume to AI-assisted research — this is explicitly addressed around `L120`, even with a real-life example cited. As something that is only tangentially related to the focus of this work (what caused many submissions vs. how to deal with many submissions), I believe this is fairly addressed.

---

### ***(6) underdeveloped details***

This concern is indeed shared by multiple reviewers (`ZGAX`, `NVPF`, `4eUb`). While I did not provide exact specifics on all aspects — as a key virtue of my framework is its innate flexibility, where I am promoting a general direction rather than a fixed set of rules — **I have in fact added a new Section 6, Recommended Practices**, offering practical guidance on how early-adopter conferences might proceed: which rules to prioritize (e.g., free registration), which to phase in later, and how to determine point valuations. I also added **Appendix B for FAQs** and **Appendix C for Case Studies**, as suggested by other reviewers.

In total, that amounts to **almost 2 new pages in the main text and 4 pages in the appendix. And all three reviewers here have either explicitly declared “questions have been resolved” or have moved on to other concerns.** If this is still not considered “addressed to a satisfactory extent,” I believe it is only fair that this be clearly elaborated in the meta-review regarding what is considered missing.

---

***(9) infeasibility of waiving registration***

This point is raised by `4eUb`, and I immediately pointed out that complimentary registration is already offered at major ML conferences, e.g., [NeurIPS offering free registrations](https://x.com/ParshinShojaee/status/1979206711882678432?s=20) to [top reviewers](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/ProgramCommittee#top-reviewer). **The reviewer explicitly acknowledged our rebuttal:**

> `4eUb`: “W4 - Registration fee costs: Thank you for the explanation. Additional details in the manuscript would be nice to see.”

**With such unequivocal facts, I honestly do not understand how this could be better addressed.** Notably, another reviewer also expressed support for this idea:

> `uVme`: “Free registration is a strong incentive and is practical for unlimited virtual registration.”

And the [upcoming ICML 2026](https://icml.cc/Conferences/2026/CallForPapers) has, in fact, adjusted its requirements to only require authors with accepted works to obtain virtual registration. While virtual passes are not free, this certainly resonates with the general design and `uVme` suggestion, and shows that conference organizers have substantial discretion in handling registration policies, as well as leeway to ensure the conference remains properly funded.


---

Frankly, as a paper dedicated to exploring better conference mechanisms, I am disappointed that it appears to have been handled with limited care, particularly in light of the OpenReview leakage incidents. Again, I do not mind the paper being rejected — it remains a statistically fair outcome — but I had hoped that, given the conference organizers’ repeated emphasis and guidance, the AC might have exercised greater due diligence in this case.

I hope that a proper update to conference review mechanisms, be that mine or another appropriate approach, will promote greater care throughout this pipeline.

Sincerely,   
*paper2457 author*
